chapters.title: The Mission
chapters.summary: Humanity's first landing on the Moon.
chapters.narration_text: In July 1969, Apollo 11 carried astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin toward the Moon. Their goal was simple and historic: land the lunar module Eagle on the surface and return safely to Earth.

chapters.title: The Machine
chapters.summary: Two stages, two different fates.
chapters.narration_text: Eagle had two parts. The descent stage held the landing engine, legs and storage, while the ascent stage carried the crew cabin and the engine that lifted the astronauts back off the Moon.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.summary: Down to the Sea of Tranquility.
chapters.narration_text: Eagle separated from the command module Columbia in lunar orbit and descended to the Sea of Tranquility. Armstrong and Aldrin touched down on July 20, 1969, while Michael Collins kept orbiting above.

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.summary: Rocks, soil and the first experiments.
chapters.narration_text: The crew collected lunar rock and soil samples and set up scientific instruments, including a laser reflector that scientists can still use to measure the distance to the Moon. The samples taught us about the Moon's early history.

chapters.title: What Remains
chapters.summary: The descent stage was left behind on purpose.
chapters.narration_text: After the moonwalk, the astronauts returned in the ascent stage. The descent stage was intentionally left on the lunar surface, and it remains at Tranquility Base today. The ascent stage is a separate story.

chapters.title: The Mission
chapters.summary: A robot scout for Apollo.
chapters.narration_text: Surveyor 3 was an uncrewed robotic lander launched in 1967. Its job was to scout the lunar surface and help NASA judge whether it was safe for future Apollo astronauts to land.

chapters.title: The Machine
chapters.summary: A camera and a scoop on three legs.
chapters.narration_text: The lander was a three-legged spacecraft with a television camera and a robotic scoop arm. It could photograph its surroundings and dig into the lunar soil to test how strong the ground was.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.summary: A soft landing on the Moon.
chapters.narration_text: Surveyor 3 launched in April 1967 and made a soft landing on the Moon a few days later, in a crater on the Ocean of Storms, then began sending pictures back to Earth.

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.summary: Proof the ground could hold a lander.
chapters.narration_text: Surveyor 3 sent back thousands of images and tested the lunar soil with its scoop. The results helped show that the Moon's surface could support a landing spacecraft and its astronauts.

chapters.title: What Remains
chapters.summary: Apollo 12 visited and took parts home.
chapters.narration_text: In 1969, Apollo 12 astronauts walked to Surveyor 3 on the Moon and retrieved several of its parts to bring back to Earth for study. The rest of the lander stayed on the Moon.

missions.name: Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle
missions.description: First Lunar Roving Vehicle driven by astronauts

chapters.title: The Mission
chapters.summary: Exploring the Moon on wheels.
chapters.narration_text: Apollo 15 launched in 1971 with a new tool for exploration: the Lunar Roving Vehicle. It would let astronauts travel far beyond walking distance from their lander, carrying tools and samples.

chapters.title: The Machine
chapters.summary: A folding electric rover.
chapters.narration_text: The rover was an electric, four-wheeled vehicle that folded up to fit on the side of the lunar module. On the Moon, the astronauts unfolded it, climbed aboard and drove across the surface.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.summary: Hadley Rille and the Apennine Mountains.
chapters.narration_text: Apollo 15 landed near the Hadley Rille and Apennine Mountains in July 1971. Astronauts David Scott and James Irwin used the rover for three days of exploring away from the lander.

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.summary: More ground, more samples.
chapters.narration_text: Driving let the crew visit more places and bring back more samples than walking alone would allow. Their rock collection included ancient lunar material that helped scientists understand how the Moon formed.

chapters.title: What Remains
chapters.summary: Left parked on the Moon.
chapters.narration_text: When the mission ended, the Lunar Roving Vehicle was left parked on the lunar surface near the landing site. It remains on the Moon today, a silent record of the first rover driven by astronauts.

chapters.title: The Mission
chapters.summary: Proving a small rover could work on Mars.
chapters.narration_text: In 1997, NASA's Mars Pathfinder mission set out to prove that a low-cost lander and a small rover could work on Mars. Sojourner was that rover, an early step in robotic exploration of the Red Planet.

chapters.title: The Machine
chapters.summary: A tiny six-wheeled rover.
chapters.narration_text: Sojourner was a small six-wheeled rover about the size of a microwave oven, powered by solar panels. It carried cameras and an instrument to study the chemical makeup of rocks.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.summary: Airbags and a ramp onto Mars.
chapters.narration_text: Pathfinder reached Mars on July 4, 1997, landing with the help of airbags. Sojourner then rolled down a ramp onto the surface and began exploring the rocky terrain around the lander.

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.summary: Real science from a small rover.
chapters.narration_text: Sojourner analyzed rocks and soil near the landing site and showed that a small rover could do real science on Mars. Its success paved the way for the larger rovers that followed.

chapters.title: What Remains
chapters.summary: Final state and location unconfirmed.
chapters.narration_text: Final contact came in September 1997. Sojourner's exact final state and location remain unconfirmed, so we do not claim to know where it stopped or what condition it is in.

chapters.title: The Mission
chapters.summary: Searching Gusev Crater for signs of water.
chapters.narration_text: In 2004, Spirit landed in Gusev Crater, a place that scientists thought might once have held a lake. Its job was to look for rocks and soils that could reveal whether Mars was once wet.

chapters.title: The Machine
chapters.summary: A robotic geologist.
chapters.narration_text: Spirit was a solar-powered, six-wheeled Mars Exploration Rover with a robotic arm, cameras and instruments for studying rocks. It worked like a robotic geologist, able to travel, look closely and analyze samples.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.summary: Far beyond the planned 90 days.
chapters.narration_text: Spirit launched in 2003 and landed on January 4, 2004. Its mission was planned for about three months, but the rover kept driving across the plains and up into the Columbia Hills for years.

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.summary: Rocks and minerals shaped by water.
chapters.narration_text: Spirit made major discoveries about Martian rocks and minerals altered by past water, revealing the geological history of Mars. Its findings helped scientists understand how water shaped the planet long ago.

chapters.title: What Remains
chapters.summary: Last contact March 2010.
chapters.narration_text: NASA's last communication with Spirit was on March 22, 2010. Recovery attempts continued for more than a year and officially ended on May 25, 2011. Spirit remains on Mars.

chapters.title: The Mission
chapters.summary: Reading the story written in Martian rock.
chapters.narration_text: Opportunity landed on Mars in January 2004, on a flat plain called Meridiani Planum. Its mission was to search for signs that water once flowed there, and to read the story written in the rocks.

chapters.title: The Machine
chapters.summary: Spirit's twin.
chapters.narration_text: Opportunity was a twin of Spirit: a solar-powered, six-wheeled rover with cameras, a robotic arm and tools to study rock and soil. It was built to last about three months.

chapters.title: The Journey
chapters.summary: Over 45 kilometers of driving.
chapters.narration_text: Opportunity far exceeded its planned lifespan, traveling over 45 kilometers across the Martian surface. It crossed plains, explored craters and kept going for more than fourteen years.

chapters.title: The Discoveries
chapters.summary: Evidence of a wetter ancient Mars.
chapters.narration_text: Opportunity found evidence that water once soaked the rocks of Meridiani Planum, helping show that ancient Mars had wetter conditions than the planet has today.

chapters.title: What Remains
chapters.summary: Silenced by a global dust storm.
chapters.narration_text: Opportunity far exceeded its planned lifespan, traveling over 45 kilometers across Mars. Final contact came on June 10, 2018, during a global dust storm. NASA declared the mission complete on February 13, 2019.
